The Oil Stress vs Inflation Expectations chart below shows the distribution of inflation expectations (10-year TIPS break-even) at the top and the distribution of oil “stress” (the scarcity premium) at the bottom. The bond market apparently believes that inflation will remain in the mid 2’s, even though the oil market is at the 100th percentile of stress.

If the conflict in Iran is resolved soon that right tail would likely move to the middle, and if that happens, the bond market will be proven correct that “this too shall pass.” But what if it doesn’t? Will that push TIPS break-evens to the right? And if that happens, will long yields move further into the danger zone?

It seemed like only a matter of time before the bond vigilantes would challenge a complacent bond market in the face of a historic oil shock that seemingly has no end in sight, and last Friday was that aha moment. The 10-year yield soared into the danger zone (above 4.5%) and the move was global, with benchmark yields in the UK, Canada, Germany, and Japan all making new cycle highs. As I have said for several years now, nothing good happens above 4.5%.

Why is 4.5-5.0% the danger zone? When the risk-free asset (Treasuries) is positively correlated to the risky asset (equities) and offers a similar yield, when that yield rises the risky asset needs to “compete” by increasing its yield as well (which means lowering its P/E ratio). That dynamic is called the Fed Model.  It was in remission during the Quantitative Easing era, but it came back in focus in 2022 when rates reset higher. It has been a driving force for equity valuations ever since.

Now the question is: who is right? The commodity complex, which is making new highs, or TIPS breakevens, which remain in their long established range?  If the TIPS market follows commodity prices higher, will long rates do the same, and will the Fed feel compelled to put that fire out through tighter policy? How will the incoming Fed Chair thread this needle, and how will the Treasury Secretary respond? What will this do to a stock market that has been carried away by the opposing right tail dynamic of an earnings boom driven by capex spending?

Ironically, both tails are “live” at the same, with investors stuck in the middle trying to navigate both extremes.

Pattern negation and stop-loss are NOT the same thing. A pattern negation can be used as a stop-loss.

A stop-loss depends on a tactical trading decision. The tighter the stop-loss below the pattern boundary the higher the risk of getting stopped out but also higher the reward/risk if the pattern succeeds. 

A logical place for a stop-loss is below the pattern boundary once the breakout is confirmed.

Stop-loss distance from the pattern boundary CAN NOT be optimized. There is no perfect stop-loss strategy that will keep you in a trade when markets get volatile. 

It is a trade off you are getting into. You need to either accept higer reward per risk but lower win%

or 

higher win% but lower reward per risk.

Choose first one if you are comfortable to be wrong quickly and more frequently in order to have few larger wins.

Investor demand for downside protection is plummeting:

The average 3-month put-to-call skew of S&P 500 single stocks is down to 0.04, the 4th-lowest reading over the last 20 years.

This measures how much more investors are paying for downside protection via put options than for upside exposure through call options.

The lower the reading, the less investors are paying to protect themselves against a market decline.

The average 3-month put-to-call skew has fallen -75% since March, posting the sharpest drop since April-May 2025.

This metric is even lower than during the 2021 meme stock frenzy.

Investors are no longer thinking about downside risk.

Global investors are cashing out of South Korean stocks:

Foreign investors have sold -$22 billion of South Korean stocks so far in May, on track for the largest monthly outflow on record.

Year-to-date, overseas investors have offloaded ~$60 billion in KOSPI stocks, on pace for the largest annual sale on record.

Most of the sales have been concentrated in Samsung and SK Hynix stocks, with ~$20 billion sold in SK Hynix alone year-to-date, including ~$12 billion so far in May.

Since November 2025, foreign investor outflows in SK Hynix have totaled ~$26.7 billion.

Global investors are one of the largest owners of South Korean equities, accounting for ~39% of the total KOSPI index market cap.

Foreign capital is exiting the world's best-performing market at an unprecedented pace.

China's economy is losing momentum:

Fixed-asset investment in China fell -1.6% YoY in the first 4 months of 2026, slipping back into contraction territory.

The decline was driven by a -13.7% year-to-date drop in property development, building on an -11.2% decline in the first 3 months of 2026.

Furthermore, industrial production rose just +4.1% YoY in April, the weakest reading since mid-2023.

At the same time, retail sales grew just +0.2% YoY, the worst reading since China's economy reopened after the pandemic in December 2022.

This comes as car sales dropped -15% YoY, the steepest decline since mid-2022.

Meanwhile, gold, silver, and jewelry sales collapsed -21% YoY, reversing sharply from the buying frenzy seen earlier this year when surging precious metal prices drove speculative demand.

China's economic slowdown is broadening.
